title: Write a Kafka Streams app that reads a topic, uppercases values, and writes to another topic.
shortTitle: Write a Kafka Streams app that reads a topic, uppercases values, and writes to another topic.

s1_definition.oneliner: Kafka Streams builds an in-app topology of source, transform, and sink, so reading a topic, uppercasing values with mapValues, and writing to another topic is just stream, mapValues, and to.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Kafka Streams** -- a client library for building stream-processing applications directly on Kafka; it runs inside your application, not a separate cluster.
- **Topology** -- a directed graph of source nodes (read from topic), processor nodes (transform), and sink nodes (write to topic).
- **mapValues** -- a stateless transformation that changes only the value, keeping the key and partition unchanged, so no repartition is needed.
- **Application ID** -- doubles as the consumer group id and names internal state and changelog topics; each distinct app must have a unique id.
- **Scaling** -- scales by partition just like a consumer group; running more instances divides the input partitions among them.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a conveyor belt at National Bank of India that carries transaction descriptions. Kafka Streams is a small worker standing by the belt who reads each slip, rewrites the description in capital letters for a standardized ledger, and places it on an outgoing belt. The worker lives inside your own office, not a separate factory, and if you add more workers they automatically split the belts between them.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
 Kafka Streams Topology
 =======================

 ┌────────────────────────┐
 │  Source Node            │
 │  raw-transactions      │
 │  (KStream)             │
 └───────────┬────────────┘
             │
             ▼
 ┌────────────────────────┐
 │  Processor Node        │
 │  mapValues(uppercase)  │
 │  (stateless transform) │
 └───────────┬────────────┘
             │
             ▼
 ┌────────────────────────┐
 │  Sink Node             │
 │  normalized-transactions│
 └────────────────────────┘


 Scaling by Partition
 =====================

  Input: 6 partitions

  ┌───────────┐ ┌───────────┐ ┌───────────┐
  │Instance 1 │ │Instance 2 │ │Instance 3 │
  │ P0, P1    │ │ P2, P3    │ │ P4, P5    │
  └───────────┘ └───────────┘ └───────────┘

  Each instance processes its assigned partitions
  Same application.id = same consumer group
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Kafka Streams is a client library for stream processing that runs inside your own application rather than a separate cluster. To read a topic, uppercase values, and write to another topic, the whole data path is three steps: stream the input, mapValues with uppercase, and write to the output. Then you build the topology, create a KafkaStreams instance, and start it.

The important choice is mapValues instead of map, because mapValues transforms only the value and keeps the key unchanged, so there is no repartition and per-account ordering is preserved. The application scales by partition just like a consumer group.

In my National Bank of India project, transaction descriptions arrived in mixed case from different channels. A small Streams app normalized them with mapValues while keeping the account key, and I unit-tested the topology with TopologyTestDriver without a running broker.

Remember one sentence: Kafka Streams is a library, not a server, and mapValues transforms values without repartitioning, so stream, mapValues, and to is the complete stateless topology.

---

keyPoints: Kafka Streams is a client library that runs inside your application, not a separate cluster.
The topology is source (stream), processor (mapValues), and sink (to) for a stateless transform.
mapValues changes only the value, keeping the key and partition unchanged with no repartition.
Application ID doubles as the consumer group id; each distinct app needs a unique id.
Scales by partition like a consumer group; running more instances divides input partitions.
TopologyTestDriver enables unit testing without a running Kafka broker.
